anti_overlap: Do not evaluate whether purged or atticked files are actually unreachable from src/index.tsx, or whether a config/tooling file still needs a deleted path — that is fd-buildgraph-reachability's domain.

Do not evaluate whether a UI surface change (the economy tab, archive tab, palette entries, agent profile modal) matches a specific mk ruling or the OUT clause — that is fd-productspec-conformance's domain, except where a type-plane bug is itself the mechanism of a rendering defect (a camelize bug that changes what a specific field displays is in scope; the tab's existence or placement is not).

Do not re-litigate whether ts-rs or generated-types-from-Rust is the right architecture — that choice is settled upstream; review only whether this plan's specific pipeline (WIRE_KEYS, camelize, mergeStatus, the postprocessing script) is implemented correctly.
decision_lens: For every stage of the pipeline (Rust struct to serde_json, IPC to TypeScript, camelize(), mergeStatus(), statusCache, hook, render), construct the concrete JSON payload that would break that stage, then check whether that payload actually occurs in the shell's real data — country ISO3 codes, commodity or agent ids used as Record keys, nested Option<T> fields, u64/i64 treasury figures, and the deployment status enum's exact string values on both the Rust and TypeScript sides. A design proven correct only against one sample fixture is not proven correct against the real data shape; treat 'the test covers the negative case chosen for the test' as insufficient evidence the positive case cannot occur.
focus: Whether the type-plane design (ts-rs generated wire types, a WIRE_KEYS-driven camelize() runtime function, the Camelize<T> mapped type, and mergeStatus/mergeStatusLight in statusCache, replacing statusNormalizer and wireFormats) has a correctness hole in Record-key collision, optional/null handling, bigint post-processing, event-name drift between Rust emit and TypeScript listen, or the deployment status vocabulary change — any of which would alter what the map or top bar actually renders.
name: fd-typegen-interop
persona: Apply the perspective of an engineer who has built and debugged cross-language serialization pipelines between Rust (serde/ts-rs) and TypeScript — someone fluent in the specific ways a generic, schema-unaware camelCase key-renaming transform corrupts data when the same JSON shape mixes typed struct fields with dynamic map keys, and in how Option<T>, u64/i64, and enum representations cross the serde boundary.
review_areas: WIRE_KEYS collision scope: WIRE_KEYS (Task 8 Step 3) is one global set scanned from every generated file's property-name tokens, and camelize() (Task 9 Step 1) renames any key wherever WIRE_KEYS.has(k) is true regardless of which struct or Record that key sits inside. The design's own docstring and test acknowledge the risk using `crude_oil` as a negative example precisely because it is not currently a wire key — verify whether any live commodity id, agent id, deployment id, or other Record key coincides with an actual generated struct field name elsewhere in the codebase today, and whether the plan gives the executor any mechanism (a lint, a test enumerating all Record-keyed maps against WIRE_KEYS) to catch a future collision rather than relying on it staying accidentally true.

Optional/nullable field handling: Rust Option<T> serializes as JSON null or an omitted key depending on serde attributes, and ts-rs represents it as `T | null` (or `T | undefined`). Verify camelize() and Camelize<T> pass null/undefined through without misrecursing or dropping the key, and that mergeStatus's '?? cached' fallbacks (Task 9 Step 2) distinguish a genuine Rust-emitted null (no data yet) from a field the incoming payload omitted entirely — if today's normalizer treated these differently and the port collapses the distinction, a field could silently keep showing stale cached data (or vice versa) after the rewrite.

bigint post-processing (Task 8 Step 3): the plan performs a text-token substitution of `bigint` to `number` across every generated .ts file. Verify this substitution is scoped to type positions only (not a field name, comment, or generic parameter containing the substring), and that treating every Rust u64/i64/usize as a JS `number` is actually safe for every newly-exported field — not just the ones the UI already displayed as approximate numbers — flagging any treasury, GDP, or population figure the top bar or a detail panel displays exactly that could exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.

Event-name drift and the criterion-9 check: verify the grep-based acceptance check for 'every listen() has a matching Rust emit' (`grep -rq "\"$e\"" crates src-tauri`) is sound against an event name built via a Rust constant or format string rather than a literal at the emit() call site — such an event would produce a false 'no emitter' failure (blocking a legitimate pass) or, if the constant's value happens to also appear as an unrelated literal string elsewhere in the tree, a silent false pass that misses genuine drift.

Deployment status vocabulary and the iso3 rename (Task 9 Step 4): the generated DeploymentStatus union replaces the old 'in-progress'/'completed' string literals via a new deploymentStatusLabel() display helper, and CountryFinanceRecord.shadow is renamed to iso3. Verify every consumer of the old string literals is actually caught by 'fix compile errors only' — an untyped comparison (`status === 'in-progress'`) inside a .tsx file with a loosely-typed prop may not raise a compile error at all, silently breaking a filter, sort comparator, or conditional style even while pnpm typecheck:web passes clean.

mergeStatus/mergeStatusLight field-level fidelity: Task 9 Step 2 requires porting the old normalizer's preferNonEmpty and '?? cached' fallback behavior 'and the old normalizer tests' onto the two new functions, naming nine fields explicitly (baselineManifest, economy, emergence, humanCapital, psychology, migration, deployments, countryNet, countryNames) — verify the plan gives the executor a way to confirm that list is exhaustive against the actual old normalizer rather than trusting the plan's own enumeration, since a field the old normalizer specially handled but the plan's list omits would silently regress to naive overwrite-or-drop behavior.

severity_examples.condition: requires a real collision between a Record key value and some generated struct's field name; severity holds regardless of how likely that specific collision is today, since nothing in the plan detects it if it occurs later
severity_examples.scenario: a commodity id, agent id, or other Record<string, T> map key in the live data coincides with an actual generated wire-struct field name, so camelize() renames a map key that should stay untouched; the map's country-GDP overlay or the economy lens's market table reads the renamed key, gets undefined for that one entry, and silently renders nothing or a stale value — the plan's own camelize test only exercises the negative case (crude_oil, chosen because it is not currently a wire key), so this defect ships past the test suite.

severity_examples.condition: a specific exported field whose real magnitude in the live sim data crosses 2^53; the plan does not audit which newly-exported fields this applies to versus the fields already displayed today
severity_examples.scenario: the blind bigint-to-number text substitution turns a u64 treasury or GDP value that can exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER into a number-typed field the top bar or a finance panel displays exactly, producing silently wrong (rounded) figures for large economies with no runtime error and no test asserting the boundary.

severity_examples.condition: any Rust emit() call whose event-name argument is not a literal string token
severity_examples.scenario: an emitted event name on the Rust side is built from a named constant or format string rather than a bare string literal at the emit() call site, so both the Task 9 Step 3 manual audit and the criterion-9 grep check miss it — a listener the shell relies on silently never fires, and every sealed acceptance criterion still passes.

success_hints: Credit Task 9's camelize test for explicitly including a Record-collision negative case (country_gdp: { USA: 1 } staying USA; a crude_oil key inside a Record staying untouched) — this shows the design is aware of the collision class even where its completeness under other/future data still needs probing.
Credit Task 8 Step 5's requirement to run pnpm generate:types twice and assert empty git porcelain the second time — a genuine idempotency check, not just an unverified claim.

Credit criterion 9's per-event emitter grep as a real automated cross-language contract check most plans of this shape skip entirely, even while noting where its literal-string assumption can be evaded.
